title: Afterschool Program
shortDescription: Structured afternoon programming with social, academic and recreational support.
description:
Afterschool programs give autistic children somewhere structured to be between the end of the school day and the end of the work day. The good ones do more than supervise: they run social skills groups, homework support, recreation, and life skills practice in a setting with a lower adult-to-child ratio and staff who understand sensory needs and behavior support.

The gap these programs fill is real. School ends around 2 or 3 in the afternoon and most parents work until 5 or later. For a child who needs predictable routine and adult support, unstructured afternoons are hard, and generic afterschool care is often a poor fit — noisy, loosely supervised, and staffed by people with no autism training.

Programs in Florida vary widely in what they actually provide. Some are run by ABA providers and deliver therapy hours in a group setting, billable to insurance. Some are recreational programs run by nonprofits or parks departments with an inclusion specialist on staff. Some are private pay day programs with a structured curriculum. These are very different things at very different prices, so ask directly: what is the staff-to-child ratio, what training do staff have, is any of this billable to insurance, and what happens when a child has a hard afternoon.

For school-age children with a Family Empowerment Scholarship for Unique Abilities (FES-UA), some afterschool and skill-building services are reimbursable. Check the current list of approved uses before assuming.
benefits: Covers the gap between school dismissal and the end of the work day
Structured routine rather than unsupervised free time
Social skills practice with peers in a supported setting
Staff trained in autism support and behavior strategies
Some programs bill insurance when delivered as group therapy
whoCanBenefit: Working parents who need supervised care after school
Children who do poorly with unstructured time
Children working on social skills with same-age peers
Families who found generic afterschool care to be a bad fit
Children who benefit from extra academic support outside the classroom
